beats.caption: Welcome! I'm Quanta. Every quantum journey starts with a single qubit.
beats.speech: Welcome! I'm Quanta. Every quantum journey starts with a single qubit. Let's meet yours.
beats.visual: Title card: module label small above, lesson title large. Quanta pops in from scale 0 with a bounce and does a small hop. Title fades out at the end of the beat; Quanta shrinks to his corner spot.

beats.caption: A classical bit is always exactly one value: 0 or 1.
beats.speech: First, a classical bit. It's always exactly one of two values: zero, or one. Flip it, and it's simply the other one.
beats.visual: A rounded box labelled 'bit' showing a big '0'. It flips (rotate around the vertical axis) to '1', then back to '0'. Each flip is crisp, and only one value is ever visible.

beats.caption: In a circuit, a qubit is a wire. Yours starts in |0⟩.
beats.speech: In a circuit, a qubit is drawn as a wire. Yours starts in the state ket zero. An empty wire means nothing has changed it yet.
beats.visual: The bit box slides away. A horizontal wire draws itself left to right, labelled 'q[0]' at the left and '|0⟩' just before the wire start. A soft glow pulse travels along the empty wire.

beats.caption: A qubit can have an amplitude for |0⟩ and for |1⟩. Square them to get the chances.
beats.speech: What makes it quantum? A qubit can have an amplitude for ket zero and an amplitude for ket one at the same time. Square their sizes, and you get the chances of each result.
beats.visual: Two vertical amplitude bars labelled |0⟩ and |1⟩ in brand colour. They start at 1.0 and 0.0 and animate to 0.6 and 0.8, with value labels following. Then each bar morphs into a probability bar (success colour) of height 0.36 and 0.64, labelled '36%' and '64%', with a small '(0.6)² = 0.36' and '(0.8)² = 0.64' note appearing under each.

beats.caption: Measurement always gives a plain 0 or 1. Many shots reveal the chances.
beats.speech: But a measurement never shows a fuzzy in-between answer. It always gives a plain zero or one. Repeat it many times, and the counts reveal those chances.
beats.visual: A measurement meter icon appears; the probability bars collapse to a single big '1' result card, then reset. Then shot dots fall one by one (accelerating) into two histogram bins '0' and '1': exactly 50 dots, 18 into 0 and 32 into 1, in a fixed deterministic order. A shot counter ticks up to 50.

beats.caption: On the Bloch sphere, up is |0⟩, down is |1⟩, and every other direction is a superposition.
beats.speech: You'll often see a qubit drawn as an arrow on a sphere. Straight up is ket zero, straight down is ket one, and every other direction is a superposition of the two.
beats.visual: A 3D-looking Bloch sphere (circle outline, equator ellipse, dashed vertical axis) with labels |0⟩ at the north pole and |1⟩ at the south pole. The state arrow points up, sweeps smoothly down through the equator to the south pole, then around and back up to the north pole.

beats.caption: Your turn: open Build, find your q[0] wire, and press Check Answer.
beats.speech: Your turn! Open Build, find your qubit zero wire, and press Check Answer when you're ready.
beats.visual: Everything fades out. Quanta returns to centre and does a happy hop; 'Your turn' appears large with the caption text below it.

beats.caption: Let's compare a classical bit with its quantum upgrade, the qubit.
beats.speech: Let's compare the smallest unit of classical information, a bit, with its quantum upgrade, the qubit.
beats.visual: Title card with Quanta pop-in, same as lesson 1.

beats.caption: A bit holds one definite value. A qubit can carry an amplitude for both |0⟩ and |1⟩.
beats.speech: A bit holds one definite value, zero or one. A qubit uses the same two labels, ket zero and ket one, but it can carry an amplitude for both.
beats.visual: Split screen with a thin vertical divider. Left, titled 'Bit': a box flipping 0 → 1 → 0. Right, titled 'Qubit': two amplitude bars |0⟩ and |1⟩ that animate from (1, 0) to (0.71, 0.71), labelled '0.71' each.

beats.caption: A superposition is not a coin that has secretly already landed.
beats.speech: A superposition is not a coin that secretly landed already, and we just haven't looked. Something genuinely different is going on.

scene.heading: A qubit is not a hidden coin

beats.visual: Clear the split screen. A coin drops under an upturned cup; a peek shows 'H' hiding underneath; then a big danger-coloured cross draws over the whole picture.

beats.caption: Amplitudes have a phase. In step they reinforce; opposite, they cancel.
beats.speech: Amplitudes have a phase, a direction. When two paths line up, they reinforce. When they point opposite ways, they cancel out. Ordinary probabilities can never cancel like that.
beats.visual: Two rows. Top row, labelled 'In step': two arrows pointing right are placed head-to-tail and merge into one arrow twice as long (success colour, label 'reinforce'). Bottom row, labelled 'Opposite': one arrow right and one arrow left are placed head-to-tail and shrink to a dot (danger colour, label 'cancel').

beats.caption: Measuring still gives one classical bit. Many shots show how often each appears.
beats.speech: Measuring still gives back one classical bit. Over many shots, the probabilities tell you how often each result appears.
beats.visual: A qubit token (circle with '|ψ⟩') moves into a meter icon and comes out as a plain bit box showing '0'. Then a shot histogram fills: exactly 40 dots, 21 into '0' and 19 into '1', in a fixed deterministic order, with a dashed 50% guide line.

beats.caption: A bit is a definite value. A qubit is a state with amplitudes that can interfere.
beats.speech: So, a bit is a definite value. A qubit is a state with amplitudes that can interfere. That's the upgrade!
beats.visual: Two summary cards side by side ('Bit: one definite value', 'Qubit: amplitudes that interfere'). Quanta hops between them, then 'Your turn' appears.

beats.caption: Charts turn invisible amplitudes into patterns you can read.
beats.speech: Charts turn invisible amplitudes into patterns you can read. Let's read three of them.
beats.visual: Title card with Quanta pop-in.

beats.caption: Our example: one qubit and an H gate, which makes an equal superposition.
beats.speech: Here's our example: one qubit with an H gate. H turns ket zero into an equal superposition.
beats.visual: The q[0] wire draws in with '|0⟩' at the start. A rounded square 'H' gate tile (brand colour) drops from above onto the wire with a slight bounce. The wire with the gate then shrinks and moves to the top strip of the frame, where it stays for the rest of the lesson.

beats.caption: Probabilities: how often each result appears. Here 50% each, and the bars sum to 100%.
beats.speech: The probability chart answers: how often will each result appear? Here it's fifty percent each, and the bars always add up to one hundred percent.
beats.visual: A probability chart with bars |0⟩ and |1⟩. They start at 100% and 0% (the state before H), then animate to 50% and 50%. A brace or line beside them shows '50% + 50% = 100%'.

beats.caption: Phase is an angle on each amplitude. Flip |1⟩ by 180° and the bars don't move.
beats.speech: Phase is an angle attached to each amplitude. Flip the phase of ket one by a hundred and eighty degrees, and the bars don't move at all. But later gates will treat these two states very differently.
beats.visual: The probability chart moves to the left half. On the right, two phase dials (circles with a pointer), one per basis state |0⟩ and |1⟩, both pointing at 0°. A 'Z' gate tile appears after H on the top-strip wire, and the |1⟩ dial rotates to 180° (label '180°'). The 50/50 bars on the left pulse to show they are unchanged, with a small 'unchanged' tag.

beats.caption: The Bloch sphere tells the same story: H tips the arrow to the equator, and the phase flip spins it to the opposite side.
beats.speech: The Bloch sphere shows the same story as geometry. H tips the arrow from the north pole down to the equator. The phase flip spins it around the equator to the opposite side.
beats.visual: Replace the chart and dials with a Bloch sphere (labels |0⟩ north, |1⟩ south, |+⟩ on the right of the equator, |−⟩ on the left). The arrow starts at north, rotates down to |+⟩ while the H tile on the top strip highlights, then rotates around the equator to |−⟩ while the Z tile highlights.

beats.caption: Three panels, one state, three questions. Your turn: add an H gate and open each chart.
beats.speech: Three panels, one state, three different questions. Your turn: add an H gate and open each chart.
beats.visual: Three small cards in a row: a mini bar chart labelled 'How often?', a mini phase dial labelled 'How do paths combine?', and a mini sphere labelled 'Where does it point?'. Quanta hops, then 'Your turn' appears.

beats.caption: A quick tour makes the Build workspace feel much less mysterious.
beats.speech: A quick tour makes the Build workspace feel much less mysterious. Let's walk through it.
beats.visual: Title card with Quanta pop-in.

beats.caption: The Gate library is on the left. The canvas holds your wires, read left to right like a timeline.
beats.speech: On the left is the Gate library, where every operation begins. In the middle is the canvas: your qubit wires, read from left to right, like a timeline.

items.title: Gates
items.body: Choose H, X, Y, Z, S, T, CX or M

beats.visual: A schematic of the workspace builds in as rounded panels: 'Gates' column on the left (a grid of small tiles H, X, Y, Z, S, T, CX, M), 'Canvas' in the centre with one wire 'q[0]', 'Inspector' on the right, and a bottom strip split into 'Results' and 'Code'. The Gates panel highlights (brand border glow) on the first sentence; the Canvas highlights on the second, while a time arrow sweeps left to right along the wire.

beats.caption: Drag H from the Gate library and drop it on q[0].
beats.speech: Drag H from the library and drop it on the qubit zero wire.
beats.visual: A cursor glyph picks the H tile from the Gates panel; a copy of the tile follows the cursor along an arc and snaps onto the q[0] wire with a small bounce.

beats.caption: Click the gate and the Inspector shows its type, target qubit and column.
beats.speech: Click the gate, and the Inspector shows exactly what it is: its type, its target qubit, and its column.
beats.visual: The cursor clicks the placed H (selection ring appears). The Inspector panel highlights and three rows type in one at a time: 'Type: H', 'Target: q[0]', 'Column: 0'.

beats.caption: Results shows what the circuit does when simulated. One H gives 50/50.
beats.speech: Results shows what the circuit does when simulated. For one H gate, that's fifty-fifty.
beats.visual: The Results panel highlights; inside it, a mini 'Probabilities' tab label and two bars |0⟩ and |1⟩ grow to 50% each.

beats.caption: Code shows the same circuit as text, ready to export: qc.h(0)
beats.speech: And Code shows the same circuit as text, ready to export. Here, the H gate is just one line.
beats.visual: The Code panel highlights and the monospace line 'qc.h(0)' types in character by character after a dim 'qc = QuantumCircuit(1)' line. A thin connector line links the H tile on the canvas to the code line.

beats.caption: Place, select, inspect. Your turn: place a gate and open each panel.
beats.speech: Place, select, inspect. That's the whole tour. Your turn: place a gate and open each panel.
beats.visual: The schematic fades back. Quanta hops to centre, and 'Your turn' appears with three chips: 'Place', 'Select', 'Inspect'.

beats.caption: Time to place your very first gate: X.
beats.speech: Time to place your very first gate. Meet X, the quantum version of NOT.

beats.caption: Your qubit starts in |0⟩, so measuring it gives 0 every time.
beats.speech: Your qubit starts in ket zero. Right now, measuring it would give zero every single time.

beats.caption: Drop X on q[0] and the state flips to |1⟩.
beats.speech: Drop an X gate on the qubit zero wire. X flips ket zero to ket one, so the bar jumps all the way across.

beats.caption: X swaps |0⟩ and |1⟩. Apply it again and you're back to |0⟩.
beats.speech: X swaps ket zero and ket one. Apply it a second time, and you're right back where you started.

beats.caption: Your turn: drag X onto the q[0] wire.
beats.speech: Your turn! Drag the X gate onto the qubit zero wire, then check your answer.

beats.caption: One H gate is all you need to create a superposition.
beats.speech: Superposition is where quantum gets interesting, and one H gate is all you need.

beats.caption: H turns |0⟩ into an equal superposition: 50% for 0, 50% for 1.
beats.speech: Place H on qubit zero. It turns ket zero into an equal superposition, with a fifty percent chance of each result.

beats.caption: Both amplitudes are positive, so both phase dials point at 0°. This is |+⟩.
beats.speech: Both amplitudes are positive, so their phases are both zero degrees. This state has a name: ket plus.

beats.caption: Measure many times and roughly half the shots land on each result.
beats.speech: If you measure it many times, about half the shots give zero and half give one. Each single shot is still random.

beats.caption: Your turn: place H on q[0] and nothing else.
beats.speech: Your turn! Place an H gate on qubit zero, and nothing else.

beats.caption: X is the quantum NOT. Let's see what it really does.
beats.speech: X is the quantum NOT gate. Let's look at what it really does.

beats.caption: On the Bloch sphere, X is a half-turn around the x-axis: north pole to south pole.
beats.speech: On the Bloch sphere, X is a half turn around the x axis. The arrow swings from the north pole, ket zero, to the south pole, ket one.

beats.caption: Like a classical NOT: 0 becomes 1, and 1 becomes 0.
beats.speech: On the basis states it acts just like a classical NOT. Zero becomes one, and one becomes zero.

beats.caption: But X on |+⟩ changes nothing: that arrow already lies on the x-axis.
beats.speech: Here's a quantum twist. Apply X to the plus state from an H gate, and nothing changes, because that arrow already lies on the x axis.

beats.caption: Your turn: apply X to flip q[0] from |0⟩ to |1⟩.
beats.speech: Your turn! Apply X to flip qubit zero from ket zero to ket one.

beats.caption: Rotation gates let you steer a qubit by any angle.
beats.speech: Rotation gates let you steer a qubit by any angle you like. Let's try R X.

beats.caption: RX(π/2) turns the arrow a quarter-turn around the x-axis, onto the equator: 50/50.
beats.speech: R X of pi over two turns the arrow a quarter turn around the x axis, from the north pole down to the equator. Now it's fifty, fifty.

beats.caption: Another RX(π/2) finishes the half-turn: now it's |1⟩.
beats.speech: Another quarter turn finishes the half turn. Two R X of pi over two make the arrow point straight down, to ket one.

beats.caption: Smaller angles mean smaller steps: RX(π/4) gives about 85% for 0 and 15% for 1.
beats.speech: Smaller angles mean smaller steps. R X of pi over four gives about eighty five percent for zero, and fifteen percent for one.

beats.caption: Your turn: place RX on q[0] with any angle.
beats.speech: Your turn! Place R X on qubit zero. Any angle counts, so experiment.

beats.caption: Not every quantum change shows up in the probabilities.
beats.speech: Not every quantum change shows up as a probability change right away. Meet the Z gate.

beats.caption: Z leaves |0⟩ alone: the arrow on the north pole doesn't move.
beats.speech: Z leaves ket zero completely alone. The arrow sits on the north pole, and Z spins it around that very axis, so nothing moves.

beats.caption: On |+⟩, Z flips the phase of |1⟩ to 180°, but the bars stay 50/50.
beats.speech: Now start with H. Z multiplies the ket one amplitude by minus one, so its phase flips to a hundred and eighty degrees. The bars stay at fifty, fifty.

beats.caption: Add another H and the hidden phase appears: H, Z, H gives 1 every time.
beats.speech: So did Z do anything? Add one more H. Interference turns that hidden phase into a real result: H, Z, H always measures one.

beats.caption: Your turn: add Z, then open the HZH walkthrough.
beats.speech: Your turn! Add a Z gate, then open the H Z H walkthrough to see phase matter.

beats.caption: S and T are small, precise phase steps.
beats.speech: S and T are small, precise phase steps. They're how we fine tune phase.

beats.caption: S adds a quarter-turn, 90°, to the phase of |1⟩.
beats.speech: Start with H, then add S. S adds a quarter turn, ninety degrees, to the phase of ket one. On the sphere, the arrow moves a quarter of the way around the equator.

beats.caption: T is half of that: an eighth-turn, 45°.
beats.speech: T is half as big, an eighth of a turn, forty five degrees.

beats.caption: Two T gates make one S, and two S gates make one Z.
beats.speech: Two T gates add up to one S, and two S gates add up to one Z. Watch the phase dial reach ninety degrees.

beats.caption: Through all of this, the probabilities stay 50/50.
beats.speech: And through all of this, the probabilities never budge. Phase gates only change how amplitudes will interfere later.

beats.caption: Your turn: place S or T and compare their phase angles.
beats.speech: Your turn! Place S or T on qubit zero and compare their phase angles.

beats.caption: Some quantum operations undo themselves when repeated.
beats.speech: Some quantum operations undo themselves when you repeat them. Hadamard is one of them.

beats.caption: One H takes |0⟩ to an equal superposition.
beats.speech: One H takes ket zero to the equator: an equal superposition.

beats.caption: A second H brings it straight back to |0⟩: H · H = I.
beats.speech: A second H brings it straight back to ket zero. H times H equals the identity, as if nothing happened.

beats.caption: The two paths to |1⟩ cancel out, while the paths to |0⟩ reinforce.
beats.speech: Why? After the second H, the two paths to ket one have opposite signs, so they cancel, while the paths to ket zero reinforce. That's interference.

beats.caption: Your turn: place H, then another H in the next column.
beats.speech: Your turn! Place an H, then another H in the next column.

beats.caption: Measurement bridges the quantum and classical worlds.
beats.speech: Measurement is the bridge between the quantum world and the classical one.

beats.caption: Measure reads q[0] and stores a classical 0 or 1 in c[0].
beats.speech: A measure gate reads qubit zero and writes the answer, a plain zero or one, into the classical bit c zero.

beats.caption: After X, the qubit is definitely |1⟩, so every shot reads 1.
beats.speech: After an X gate, the qubit is definitely in ket one, so every single shot reads one.

beats.caption: Each shot gives a plain 0 or 1, and the qubit is left in the state you saw.
beats.speech: Two rules to remember. Each shot gives a plain zero or one. And afterwards, the qubit is left in the state you just saw.

items.title: It collapses
items.body: Afterwards the qubit is in the state you saw

beats.caption: Your turn: drag Measure onto q[0]. It links to c[0].
beats.speech: Your turn! Drag the measure gate onto qubit zero. It links to c zero automatically.

lessons.title: Run Shots and Read a Histogram

beats.caption: One run is a sample; many shots reveal the distribution.
beats.speech: One run is just a sample. Many shots reveal the whole distribution.

beats.caption: H then measure: the ideal chances are 50% each.
beats.speech: Here's H followed by a measurement. In theory, each result has a fifty percent chance.

beats.caption: With only 10 shots you might see 6 and 4. Small samples are noisy.
beats.speech: With only ten shots, you might see six zeros and four ones. Small samples are noisy.

beats.caption: With 8,192 shots the histogram settles close to 50/50.
beats.speech: With eight thousand one hundred ninety two shots, the histogram settles very close to fifty, fifty.

beats.caption: Your turn: add a measurement, then use Run to collect shots.
beats.speech: Your turn! Add a measurement, then use Run to collect shots. Try more shots for a steadier histogram.

beats.caption: Let's turn a quantum possibility into a classical result.
beats.speech: Let's turn a quantum possibility into a classical result.

beats.caption: First prepare: H puts q[0] into an equal superposition.
beats.speech: First, prepare. H puts qubit zero into an equal superposition.

beats.caption: Then measure: each shot picks 0 or 1 at random.
beats.speech: Then measure. Each shot randomly picks zero or one, and the superposition is gone.

beats.caption: Repeat the experiment and a 50/50 histogram builds up.
beats.speech: Repeat the whole experiment many times, and a fifty, fifty histogram builds up.

beats.caption: Order matters: measuring before H always gives 0.
beats.speech: Order matters. If you measure before the H, you're measuring ket zero, so you'd always get zero.

beats.caption: Your turn: place H first and Measure second.
beats.speech: Your turn! Place H first, and measure second.

beats.caption: Ideal math is neat. Real hardware adds a little static.
beats.speech: Ideal math is neat. Real hardware adds a little static. Let's see how.

beats.caption: The Bell circuit: H, then CX. Ideally only 00 and 11 appear.
beats.speech: Here's the Bell circuit: H, then a C X. In an ideal simulation, only zero zero and one one ever appear.

beats.caption: Ideal: about half 00, half 11, and nothing else.
beats.speech: Run it ideally, and you get about half zero zero, half one one, and nothing else.

beats.caption: With realistic noise, a few 01 and 10 results sneak in.
beats.speech: Now add realistic noise. A few zero one and one zero results sneak in. These are errors.

beats.caption: Gate noise and readout errors cause the extra results.
beats.speech: They come from two places: gates that are slightly imperfect, and readout errors, where a zero is read as a one.

beats.caption: Your turn: build the Bell circuit, then Run with Realistic noise.
beats.speech: Your turn! Build the Bell circuit, then run it with the realistic noise preset.

beats.caption: Adding one qubit doubles the number of basis states.
beats.speech: Adding just one qubit doubles the number of basis states. Let's meet all four.

beats.caption: Two qubits have four basis states: 00, 01, 10 and 11.
beats.speech: Two qubits have four basis states. Each label is a two bit string, one bit per qubit.

beats.caption: Labels read like Qiskit: q[0] is the right bit, so X on q[0] gives 01.
beats.speech: Labels read like Qiskit, with qubit zero as the rightmost bit. So an X on qubit zero gives zero one.

beats.caption: Flip q[1] as well and you reach 11.
beats.speech: Flip qubit one as well, and you reach one one.

beats.caption: H on both qubits spreads the state evenly: 25% each.
beats.speech: Put H on both qubits, and the state spreads evenly across all four, twenty five percent each.

beats.caption: Every new qubit doubles the count: n qubits have 2ⁿ states.
beats.speech: Every new qubit doubles the count. Three qubits have eight states, and n qubits have two to the n.

beats.caption: Your turn: add a second qubit and inspect all four states.
beats.speech: Your turn! Add a second qubit, then inspect all four states in the results panel.

beats.caption: Now qubits can condition one another.
beats.speech: Now qubits can condition one another. Meet the controlled X gate.

beats.caption: CX flips its target only when its control is 1. Here q[0] is 0, so nothing happens.
beats.speech: C X flips its target only when its control is one. Here qubit zero is zero, so nothing happens.

beats.caption: Set the control to 1 with X, and CX flips q[1]: 01 becomes 11.
beats.speech: Set the control to one with an X gate, and now C X flips qubit one. Zero one becomes one one.

beats.caption: With q[0] as control: 00 and 10 stay put, 01 and 11 swap.
beats.speech: Here's the full table. When the control is zero, nothing changes. When it's one, the target bit flips.

beats.caption: With a superposed control, CX creates entanglement: 00 and 11.
beats.speech: And if the control is in superposition, C X creates entanglement. Only zero zero and one one remain.

beats.caption: Your turn: place CX with q[0] as control and q[1] as target.
beats.speech: Your turn! Place C X with qubit zero as the control and qubit one as the target.

beats.caption: Two gates, two different kinds of coordination.
beats.speech: Two gates, two very different kinds of coordination: C Z and SWAP.

beats.caption: CZ flips the phase of 11 to 180°. The bars don't move.
beats.speech: C Z flips the phase of one one, and only one one. The bars don't move, but its phase dial jumps to a hundred and eighty degrees.

beats.caption: CZ is symmetric: it only cares whether both qubits are 1.
beats.speech: C Z is symmetric. There's no real difference between control and target. It only cares whether both qubits are one.

items.title: Only 11 changes
items.body: It picks up a minus sign

beats.caption: SWAP exchanges two qubits: 01 becomes 10.
beats.speech: SWAP is different. It exchanges the complete states of two qubits. Here, zero one becomes one zero.

beats.caption: In Qiskit, they're qc.cz(0, 1) and qc.swap(0, 1).
beats.speech: In Qiskit code, they're written as q c dot c z, and q c dot swap.

beats.caption: Your turn: try CZ or SWAP and inspect what changes.
beats.speech: Your turn! Try C Z or SWAP, and inspect what changes.

beats.caption: Two conditions can control one flip.
beats.speech: Two conditions can control one flip. That's the Toffoli gate, also called C C X.

beats.caption: CCX flips q[2] only when q[0] and q[1] are both 1. Here they're 0.
beats.speech: C C X flips qubit two only when qubit zero and qubit one are both one. Here they're both zero, so nothing changes.

beats.caption: One control on isn't enough: 001 stays 001.
beats.speech: Turn on just one control, and it's still not enough. Zero zero one stays zero zero one.

beats.caption: Both controls on: q[2] flips, and 011 becomes 111.
beats.speech: Turn on both controls, and now qubit two flips. Zero one one becomes one one one.

beats.caption: Toffoli computes AND reversibly, a building block of classical logic.
beats.speech: Toffoli computes a logical AND without losing information, which makes it a key building block for reversible logic.

items.title: Classical AND
items.body: q[2] flips when q[0] AND q[1]

items.title: Reversible
items.body: Apply it twice and you undo it

beats.caption: Your turn: use q[0] and q[1] as controls and q[2] as target.
beats.speech: Your turn! Use qubit zero and qubit one as controls, and qubit two as the target.

beats.caption: Two qubits, one entangled pair. Let's build a Bell state!
beats.speech: Two qubits, one entangled pair. Let's build a Bell state.

beats.caption: Step one: H on q[0] makes 00 and 01 equally likely.
beats.speech: Step one. Put H on qubit zero. Now zero zero and zero one are equally likely.

beats.caption: Step two: CX from q[0] to q[1] turns 01 into 11.
beats.speech: Step two. Add C X from qubit zero to qubit one. It turns zero one into one one, leaving zero zero and one one.

beats.caption: Measure both: always 00 or 11, never a mix.
beats.speech: Measure both qubits and you always get matching results: zero zero, or one one. Never a mix.

beats.caption: Each qubit alone is random, yet together they always agree.
beats.speech: Each qubit on its own looks completely random, yet together they always agree. That's entanglement.

beats.caption: Your turn: H on q[0], then CX from q[0] to q[1].
beats.speech: Your turn! Place H on qubit zero, then a C X from qubit zero to qubit one.

beats.caption: Entanglement: two qubits, one shared quantum story.
beats.speech: Entanglement means two qubits share one quantum story. There's more than one way to create it.

beats.caption: Flip the roles: H on q[1], then CX from q[1] to q[0].
beats.speech: Flip the roles. Put H on qubit one, then a C X controlled by qubit one. Again, only zero zero and one one remain.

beats.caption: Start q[1] at 1 and you get 01 and 10: they always disagree.
beats.speech: Start qubit one at one, and you get zero one and one zero instead. Now the qubits always disagree, but they're still entangled.

beats.caption: If you can't describe each qubit on its own, they're entangled.
beats.speech: Here's the test. If you can't describe each qubit separately, they're entangled. H on both qubits alone doesn't count.

items.title: Entangled
items.body: You can't describe each qubit separately

items.title: Not entangled
